My sister Pema doesn't usually make spreadsheets for fun, so I knew something was up when she took over the dining table for a whole weekend.
She had printed emails, dated photos of the chemical drums behind the plant, and a timeline in two columns: 'What happened' and 'Who I told'. When I asked, she said, 'Only facts, Varun. No adjectives.'
On Monday she took leave and went to see a lawyer who works with a whistleblower support group. She came back quieter but steadier, with a list of protections I hadn't known existed.
On Wednesday she filed a report with the state pollution control board and saved a copy of everything she sent.
I don't know how scared she was. She didn't say. She just ate two plates of rice that night and slept eleven hours.

Sunaina, you're asking whether to go outside the company. Let me tell you what Ujjwal did at twenty-six, when the internal route failed.
I was a site engineer at a housing project in Ranchi. The steel in the columns wasn't what the drawings said. I wrote to my manager, then to the head office quality team, with photos and test certificates. Nothing. Then I was taken off the site.
I was frightened, but people were going to live in those buildings. So I didn't write angry posts. I went first to a lawyer at a legal aid centre, a patient woman who explained what protections existed. She told me: facts, not opinions. Dates, documents, photographs.
With her help I sent a formal complaint to the state building authority. Inspectors came within a month and stopped work on two towers.
It cost me that job. But the columns were rebuilt. That choice, to get proper advice before acting, is the one I'm proudest of.

qa.a: A lawyer at a legal aid centre.

qa.a: Ujjwal felt frightened of the cost, but deeply concerned for the people who would live in those buildings.

qa.a: Getting proper legal advice first, then documenting facts rather than opinions before complaining to the building authority.

Swati had forty-eight hours. The pharmaceutical company had sent her a letter: sign a confidentiality agreement and resign quietly, or face "disciplinary action". Her complaint to the internal ethics office about altered stability data had gone unanswered for three months. And the batch was due to ship next week.
She wanted to post everything online. Instead she called Divyansh, a college friend who now worked at a legal aid clinic in Ahmedabad. He said, "Don't sign anything yet. Don't post anything. Come in tomorrow with your documents."
At the clinic, a senior lawyer went through her timeline with her: dates, emails, the data files, the unanswered complaint. "Facts, not adjectives," she said. She explained, in general terms, what protections might apply, and helped Swati prepare a report to the drug regulator.
Swati submitted it the next evening, an hour before the deadline. Her hands shook as she pressed send. But for the first time in months, she felt steady.

qa.a: Forty-eight hours.

qa.a: She felt nervous, hands shaking, but steady for the first time in months.

After his internal complaint about the waste-dumping went nowhere and his manager began freezing him out, Akash sat in a small legal aid office in Kolkata with a thick folder on his knees.
Dolma, the lawyer, didn't rush him. She asked for dates, then documents, then photographs, and put aside everything that was opinion. "Anger is understandable," she said. "But the authorities act on facts."
She explained, in plain words, what protection bodies existed and how to approach them, and warned him not to take any company files he wasn't entitled to. Together they drafted a report for the pollution control board, keeping only what he had seen himself.
When he signed it, Akash felt afraid, and also clear. He called his parents that night and told them what he had done. His father, after a long silence, said, "We'll manage. You did the right thing."
Three weeks later, officials inspected the site.

qa.a: He felt afraid, and also clear, knowing he had taken the proper step.

qa.a: Taking legal advice, documenting facts he had seen himself, avoiding opinions, and reporting to the proper authority.
